name: GABON

flag.title: Flag of Gabon
flag.note: Green, yellow & blue — forest, sun, ocean

lead: Gabon is on Africa's Atlantic coast, where the Equator crosses ancient rainforest. Over 80% of the land is jungle. Forest elephants, silverback gorillas and mandrills live there. The mandrill is the world's most colourful monkey. Gabon has kept most of its trees standing. They soak up huge amounts of carbon.

facts.sub: about the size of New Zealand

sections.geography: A forest on the ocean's edge
sections.wows: 7 things to make you go wow

geo: Gabon straddles the Equator on Central Africa's Atlantic coast. Thick rainforest covers over 80% of the land. The Ogooué River winds 1,200 km to the sea. It has been Gabon's highway for centuries.

The coast mixes white-sand beaches, mangrove swamps and rocky coves. Inland, hills rise to the Chaillu Massif. Lopé National Park lies there, with ancient savanna ringed by jungle. UNESCO has named it a World Heritage Site.
animals: Gabon shelters nearly 85,000 forest elephants, more than any other country. In Loango National Park, they stroll along the beach. Waves lap at their feet. Hippos body-surf in the sea nearby.

The mandrill is the world's largest monkey, with a vivid red-and-blue face. It is Gabon's national animal. Around 35,000 western lowland gorillas live in the forests. Lopé has the biggest mandrill troop ever recorded, over 1,400 strong.
culture: Gabon has more than 40 ethnic groups. The largest is the Fang. The Bwiti spiritual tradition mixes ancestor worship, drumming and the sacred iboga plant. Iboga is a rainforest shrub. Scientists study it as a possible medicine for addiction.

Music fills village life. The mvet harp-lute and the wooden obala xylophone set the beat at festivals. Meals mix French influence with forest flavours. People eat smoked fish, cassava and plantain. On the coast, there is fresh lobster.
history: Portuguese sailors arrived in 1472. They named the estuary 'Gabão' for its cloak-like shape. France colonised Gabon in the 1800s. Freed enslaved people founded Libreville. Its name means 'free town'.

Gabon won independence on 17 August 1960. Oil money in the 1970s made it one of Africa's richer nations. In 2021 it became the first African country paid cash for protecting its forests. It received $17 million under the UN's REDD+ programme.
wows: Gabon absorbs more CO₂ than it produces, so it is a net carbon sink.
In Loango you can see elephants on the beach, hippos surfing and whales offshore, all in one day.
Gabon made the iboga plant part of its national heritage in 2000, and scientists now study it for addiction.
In 2002 Gabon created 13 national parks at once, protecting 11% of its land.
Forest elephants are Gabon's 'mega-gardeners', spreading seeds far and wide in their dung.
Lopé has 1,800 ancient rock carvings alongside gorillas, a rare natural and cultural UNESCO site.
Gabon's flag has a rare 3:4 ratio, shared with only a few countries such as DR Congo.

myths.fact: Gorillas are shy plant-eaters. Chest-beating is a show to warn rivals, and real fights are rare.

myths.myth: All African elephants are the same
myths.fact: Gabon's forest elephant is a separate species. It is smaller, with straighter tusks, and lives deep in the jungle far from the savanna elephants most people picture.
